description: PROJECT CYGNUS is an independent space exploration initiative driven by curiosity, scientific discovery, and innovation. We leverage data, technology, and creativity to transform space-related challenges into meaningful solutions.
summary:
ARIA (Martian Exploration & Navigation System) is a map-centred planetary exploration and decision-support prototype developed for the challenge “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map.”

ARIA brings together whole-planet exploration, 2D mapping, 3D terrain visualisation, geological and hazard markers, terrain-aware route planning, traverse simulation and emergency response assessment in one interface. Its navigation engine uses weighted A* pathfinding to compare routes based on distance, slope, surface difficulty and terrain uncertainty. Users can inspect environmental context, simulate mission disruptions, estimate resource consumption and evaluate recovery options using candidate emergency hubs.

ARIA also includes offline exploration capabilities, allowing essential mapping and simplified route planning to continue without an internet connection.

The project aims to make complex planetary information easier to interpret and support better-informed exploration decisions. It is a prototype for mission-planning research and education, not a certified navigation or human-safety system.
details:
ARIA is a browser-based Martian exploration and navigation system designed to connect planetary mapping, terrain intelligence, mission planning and emergency response through a unified interface.

Planetary Exploration

ARIA provides three interconnected viewing modes:

  • 2D Map: Search and explore Martian locations, geological features, hazard zones, science markers, resources, rover positions, relay hubs and saved places.
  • 3D Terrain: Navigate a perspective surface environment to inspect craters, slopes, valleys and terrain features.
  • Globe: Explore Mars at planetary scale, including illumination, day/night transitions and illustrative orbital elements.

Terrain Intelligence

The system provides elevation, slope and traversal-cost representations to help users interpret surface difficulty. Obstacle categories include steep terrain, loose rubble, soft ground, crater walls, dust-related conditions and unmapped areas. Scientific and resource-interest markers provide additional planetary context.

Intelligent Navigation

ARIA uses a weighted A* pathfinding algorithm with 16 movement directions. Its terrain-cost model considers movement distance, slope, surface difficulty, obstacles and uncertainty. Users can define starting and destination points, compare route alternatives, inspect terrain profiles and review estimated travel time.

Traverse Simulation

Users can simulate an expedition along a selected route, monitor estimated mission resources and introduce what-if events such as dust storms, blocked paths, equipment faults and low-oxygen situations.

Emergency Response and Communication

The Emergency Location & Response System (ELRS) assesses an incident using a last-known or manually entered position, remaining supplies and candidate recovery hubs. Satellite-contact locations are intended to provide additional communication-planning context. These are candidate locations, not guaranteed communication links or verified shelters.

Offline Capability

ARIA uses browser caching and local storage to retain essential application resources. Its offline mode supports the cached planetary model, catalogue, exploration interface and a coarser on-device route planner.

Technology

The project uses JavaScript ES modules, HTML, CSS, WebGL2 and GLSL for the frontend and planetary visualisation; Python and Starlette for backend services; and terrain-processing, pathfinding, simulation and data-validation components. Browser storage and Service Workers support offline functionality.

Creativity and Intended Impact

ARIA's central idea is to connect exploration, analysis, navigation, simulation and emergency assessment instead of treating them as separate tools. It demonstrates how planetary information can be presented as an interactive field environment that encourages more informed exploration decisions.

Current Limitations

The bundled global terrain is a deterministic model, not a measured global NASA DEM. Some environmental values and demonstration records are simulated or modelled. Relay hubs are fictional demonstration locations, and resource estimates are based on assumptions. ARIA is an educational and decision-support prototype, not an operational or certified human-safety system.
